impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents, which cover the use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headaches. A jury had found willful infringement by Lilly and no invalidity, but the district court overturned the verdict on written description and enablement grounds. This decision restores patent protection for a significant migraine treatment franchise.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to claim genus-level antibody inventions where the specification discloses methods of making the claimed antibodies and at least one specific embodiment, reinforcing protection for blockbuster biologic drug patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face continued patent barriers to market entry for anti-CGRP antibody therapies, potentially extending branded drug exclusivity and higher drug costs.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not included in a prior IPR petition, based on the 'reasonably could have raised' standard.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and inadequate accounting for hindsight bias in estopping another. The court clarified the evidentiary standard for determining what a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered when evaluating IPR estoppel in district court litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants in patent litigation greater ability to raise invalidity defenses that were not included in prior IPR petitions, limiting the reach of IPR estoppel and preserving more avenues for challenging patent validity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face reduced benefit from IPR estoppel, as accused infringers may have more latitude to assert invalidity grounds in district court even after IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that each of the four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether the patent invalidity finding should be reversed where the alleged inventive contribution consisted of generally known ideas.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding the alleged inventive contribution consisted of generally known ideas. The counterfeiting claim and associated damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that companies accused of trade secret misappropriation can challenge protectability by showing that claimed secrets are generally known in the industry, providing a strong defense.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret claimants must rigorously establish that their asserted secrets are not generally known; failure to do so can result in complete reversal of jury verdicts and loss of injunctive relief.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) had expired before Insulet brought suit, where Insulet had knowledge of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's judgment in favor of Insulet on its DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim, holding that the three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation well before the limitations period began. This eliminated the damages award and permanent injunction against EOFlow.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for companies accused of trade secret theft that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations is strictly enforced, offering a strong defense when plaintiffs delay filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners risk losing their claims entirely if they fail to act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation, even when ongoing harm continues.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award, where the software licensor alleged misappropriation of configuration software trade secrets.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding that the district court improperly excluded two damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the court's recognition that multiple damages methodologies may be appropriate in trade secret cases and that jury verdicts on contract damages should not be lightly overturned.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop software while licensing third-party technology face significant misappropriation risk and potential damages exposure if they create competing products using knowledge gained during the license relationship.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent applicant's change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional application constituted a correction of an obvious typographical error entitled to the provisional's priority date, or whether it introduced new matter that broke the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity of Enanta's '953 patent, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in a chemical substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error and therefore the patent could not claim priority from the provisional application. This allowed Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid's active ingredient) to serve as anticipating prior art. The decision invalidates Enanta's patent claims covering Pfizer's blockbuster COVID-19 treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects companies like Pfizer from patent claims where the patent holder's priority chain is broken by imprecise provisional application drafting, preserving freedom to operate for products disclosed between provisional and non-provisional filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face heightened risk that even minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications will be treated as new matter rather than correctable errors, potentially destroying priority and enabling anticipation by intervening disclosures.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to independently sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to independently bring infringement actions against third parties possesses a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license. The court found the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring licensing agreements can retain enforcement rights and maintain standing to sue infringers independently, providing flexibility in patent monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot as easily challenge standing based on the existence of an exclusive license when the patent owner has retained meaningful enforcement rights.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single jury verdict question covering infringement for all asserted patents, and whether the court properly analyzed patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 for patents directed to wireless building automation system improvements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments against ecobee for smart thermostat patents, finding that the use of a single verdict form question covering all asserted patents was prejudicial error requiring a new trial. The court also remanded for further Alice step two analysis on one patent while affirming eligibility for others. The decision addresses both procedural requirements for multi-patent trials and § 101 eligibility for IoT/building automation technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in multi-patent cases benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately identify which patents are infringed, preventing ambiguous aggregate verdicts that obscure the basis for liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face increased procedural complexity and risk of new trials if verdict forms do not require patent-by-patent findings of infringement.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality where the accused multicore processor selection method was largely performed abroad, and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of a patent relating to multicore processor task allocation. The court's ruling on extraterritoriality and doctrine of equivalents has significant implications for semiconductor and technology companies whose products and methods span multiple jurisdictions. The court also addressed the striking of damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies with global operations benefit from clarity on extraterritorial limits of U.S. patent infringement, potentially shielding foreign-performed method steps from domestic patent liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting method claims face challenges when accused processes are performed partly or wholly outside the United States, limiting their ability to enforce patents against global technology products.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for automated farming data collection, processing, and sharing are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data automation patents were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional for purposes of attorney fee shifting. The decision impacts agricultural technology companies seeking patent protection for data collection and processing systems attached to farming equipment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech companies accused of infringement benefit from the affirmation that automated data collection and sharing claims may be patent-ineligible, and may recover fees in exceptional cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies developing precision agriculture and farming IoT technologies face heightened § 101 eligibility challenges and risk fee exposure if their patent assertions are found to make the case exceptional.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify about matters outside personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether source code constitutes hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence, in the context of an on-sale bar defense under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) deposition testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge and that computer source code is not hearsay. This clarifies important evidentiary standards for patent invalidity defenses based on prior commercial sales of software-enabled devices.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants asserting prior art defenses benefit from the ruling that corporate representative testimony and source code are admissible evidence at summary judgment, easing the burden of proving on-sale bar invalidity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges where the prior art product was sold commercially, as courts may admit broader categories of evidence including corporate testimony and source code.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation to refer to the compounds in any form (including salt forms), and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, upholding the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that equitable considerations alone do not justify dispensing with a bond pending appeal. The decision protects branded pharmaceutical exclusivity while reinforcing bond requirements in preliminary injunction cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmation that claim terms referring to drug compounds encompass salt forms, strengthening patent protection against generic entry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Preliminary injunction plaintiffs must post a bond pending appeal even when equities strongly favor them, increasing the cost of enforcing patent rights against generic competitors.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility determination for some asserted patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, in a case involving digital communication technology using non-uniform signal constellations. The court affirmed infringement and damages findings, including the denial of motions to exclude damages expert testimony. The decision impacts the telecommunications and consumer electronics industries regarding patentability of signal processing innovations incorporated into standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmation that certain claims directed to improved signal constellations are patent-eligible, and that damages expert testimony based on reasonable royalty methodology is admissible.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers face continued exposure to patent infringement claims for implementing standard-essential technologies, with some eligibility questions remaining unresolved on remand.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination of patent claims directed to sensor-based logistics systems with time-delayed reporting, and whether a third party's IPR petition filed on the deadline of the sued party raises procedural concerns.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved a potentially strategic IPR filing by Qualcomm, which was not a party to the underlying litigation but filed petitions challenging patents asserted against Roambee on the last day of Roambee's filing deadline. The decision addresses both the substantive obviousness analysis and the procedural boundaries of third-party IPR petitions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the court's closer scrutiny of obviousness determinations and the potential limitation on strategic third-party IPR filings designed to circumvent time bars.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR as a defense strategy face uncertainty about whether third-party petitions filed near statutory deadlines will be sustained, potentially requiring additional litigation investment.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement complaint on the pleadings based on obviousness where the PTAB previously invalidated related claims of the same patent on the same grounds, and whether such a case qualifies as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement case involving unified electronic banking system claims on obviousness grounds, but reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 sanctions against counsel. The court held that while the complaint was properly dismissed because the surviving claims were invalid on the same grounds as those cancelled in IPR, the case did not meet the exceptional case standard for fee shifting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases can seek early dismissal based on obviousness when the PTAB has already invalidated related claims of the same patent, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: The reversal of fee awards signals that even weak patent assertions may not automatically qualify as exceptional, limiting defendants' ability to recover litigation costs in borderline cases.
